question_text: A 16-year-old male adolescent presents to his pediatrician with increasing fatigue and breathlessness with exercise. His parents inform the doctor that they have recently migrated from a developing country, where he was diagnosed as having a large ventricular septal defect (VSD). However, due to their poor economic condition and scarce medical facilities, surgical repair was not performed in that country. The pediatrician explains to the parents that patients with large VSDs are at increased risk for several complications, including Eisenmenger syndrome. If the patient has developed this complication, he is not a good candidate for surgical closure of the defect. Which of the following clinical signs, if present on physical examination, would suggest the presence of this complication?

                    ### Question
                    A 16-year-old male adolescent presents to his pediatrician with increasing fatigue and breathlessness with exercise. His parents inform the doctor that they have recently migrated from a developing country, where he was diagnosed as having a large ventricular septal defect (VSD). However, due to their poor economic condition and scarce medical facilities, surgical repair was not performed in that country. The pediatrician explains to the parents that patients with large VSDs are at increased risk for several complications, including Eisenmenger syndrome. If the patient has developed this complication, he is not a good candidate for surgical closure of the defect. Which of the following clinical signs, if present on physical examination, would suggest the presence of this complication?

                    ### Options
                    opa. A loud first heart sound
opb. A mid-diastolic low-pitched rumble at the apex
opc. Right ventricular heave
opd. Prominence of the left precordium
ope. Lateral displacement of the apical impulse

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
A loud first heart sound is not indicative of Eisenmenger syndrome. A mid-diastolic low-pitched rumble at the apex is not specific to this condition. Right ventricular heave, which can result from right ventricular hypertrophy due to pulmonary hypertension in Eisenmenger syndrome, is a key physical finding. Prominence of the left precordium is associated with right ventricular heave. Lateral displacement of the apical impulse is not a characteristic feature of Eisenmenger syndrome.
